summary: This proposed standard captures the semantics of the Footprint and Capabilities Advertisement part of the CDNI Request Routing interface, meaning what Footprint and Capabilities should mean in the CDNI context and what the advertisement interface offers.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC defines the information one content delivery network can advertise to another about coverage and supported features. It gives the advertisements a shared structure while leaving their transport protocol to other documents.

subtitle: Defines what CDNI footprint and capability advertisements mean, and how their objects can be extended.

tldr.problem: An upstream CDN needs consistent information about where a downstream CDN can deliver and which features it supports.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines footprint and capability semantics, a JSON base object, five initial capability types and rules for future extensions.
tldr.outcome: It defines advertisement meaning and security requirements but leaves the transport protocol to other documents. RFC 9388 later updates it.

facts.label: Initial capability types
facts.value: Delivery, Acquisition, Redirection Mode, Logging and Metadata

today: RFC 8008 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 9388. It defines advertisement semantics and objects, while leaving the transport protocol to other documents.

sections.title: The Footprint and Capabilities Interface
sections.content:
Content Delivery Network Interconnection (CDNI) allows multiple content delivery networks to cooperate. In the Footprint and Capabilities Advertisement interface (FCI), a downstream CDN (dCDN) tells an upstream CDN (uCDN) about its coverage and features.

This RFC defines the meaning of those advertisements and gives guidance for protocols that carry them. It assumes the CDNs have already connected and can exchange information; choosing a specific transport protocol is outside its scope.
sections.plainLanguage: A downstream CDN can tell an upstream CDN where it is willing to serve requests and what it can do. This RFC defines what those statements mean, not how the networks send them.

sections.title: What Footprint and Capability Mean
sections.content:
A footprint describes the area from which client requests may originate and to which a CDN is willing to deliver content. It can use address ranges, network identifiers, country codes or coordinates. This RFC defines how known footprint descriptions are carried, not which description method is best.

A capability is a feature that the uCDN relies on when deciding whether to delegate a request. Support may change over time and may apply only to part of a dCDN's footprint.
sections.plainLanguage: A footprint describes where a CDN can serve requests. A capability describes a feature that the upstream CDN can rely on when it delegates a request.

sections.title: Capabilities Restricted by Footprint
sections.content:
The RFC chooses the model of capabilities with footprint restrictions. An advertisement can state that a capability applies only in certain areas. The footprints act as constraints on delegation, and multiple footprint constraints narrow the eligible area cumulatively.

The FCI mainly carries updates to coverage and capabilities already established between the CDNs. Detailed, highly dynamic information such as current load or delivery latency is outside its scope.
sections.plainLanguage: A capability may apply only in some areas, so the upstream CDN checks both the feature and its footprint. The interface focuses on changes to agreed coverage and capabilities, not constantly changing performance data.

sections.title: The Advertisement Object
sections.content:
The base object contains a required capability-type and a required capability-value. It may also include a list of footprints that restrict where the capability applies. Objects use JSON and follow the I-JSON recommendations; property names defined by this RFC are lowercase.

The initial capability objects describe delivery protocols, acquisition protocols, redirection modes, logging support and metadata support. The format of the capability value depends on its type.
sections.plainLanguage: Each object identifies its capability type and gives the value for that type. A list of footprints can limit where the capability applies.

sections.title: Extending Capability Types
sections.content:
Future specifications may add footprint and capability types. Each initial capability has an FCI-prefixed payload type. A changed capability object must use a newly registered payload type to identify its version.

An FCI protocol must define how peers handle optional types they do not support. An upstream CDN may ignore an unknown type and decide using the information it understands. IANA established a registry for redirection modes, including DNS-I, DNS-R, HTTP-I and HTTP-R.
sections.plainLanguage: The list of capability types can grow through registered additions. A peer can skip an unfamiliar optional type and use the information it recognizes.

sections.title: Security Requirements for Advertisement Protocols
sections.content:
Because the RFC does not define a transport protocol, it states security requirements for protocols that carry the advertisements. They must provide integrity and authentication so an attacker cannot forge a false footprint or capability advertisement.

They must also provide confidentiality because a dCDN may share outage or coverage information with its uCDN but not with competing CDNs. The RFC says transport-layer security with domain certificates could meet these requirements.
sections.plainLanguage: The protocol carrying advertisements must prove who sent them and protect them from changes. It must also keep the information private from other CDNs.

items.text: Protocols used to deliver content to an end user.

items.title: Acquisition Protocol
items.text: Protocols used to obtain content from the uCDN or origin.

items.text: Supported DNS or HTTP redirection modes.
